The count has no total of districts beside it, no system worked in is named, and nothing is held on governance or on the twelve months to the as-at.

short: Internet kits and subscriptions were handed to 23 communes in 2026; whether the links are in service and the total of communes are not known.
gaps: No source says a commune's link is in service: the 23 Starlink kits and subscriptions are reported as handed over (TCD-006, TCD-007), and 23 is a count with no national total of communes. TCD-005 lists municipalities among the points sending civil registration data by SMS, with no count, no place outside the capital, no statement that it is past a pilot and no connection provided to the office. TCD-001's plan is for 2027 and TCD-002 gives no period, so plan:current rests on a project whose dates the facts do not state.

short: A birth-records platform was at pilot in four communes in 2026 and town hall fibre had not begun; how town halls connect is not known.
gaps: No source states how any town hall is connected: the only institutional connection on record (TGO-002) is PDiMa/PANT's planned fibre to 136 town hall buildings, and TGO-018 (July 2026) says works had not begun and gives no figure for town halls connected by other means. The authorities facts disagree: none under the programme (TGO-018, TGO-001, TGO-019), a pilot in the four communes of Vo (TGO-015, May 2026) and in Golfe 3 in Grand Lomé (TGO-010, 2024), and one commune, Lacs 1, on a commune application in 2021 with no total (TGO-013).

short: Sixteen municipalities worked in a national permit system in 2026; how many municipalities have a connected office is not known.
gaps: No share or count of municipalities connected is published and no total of municipalities is given: the 16 on Taamir are a count without its denominator, and the 71 per cent of sites on the administrative network in 2024 (TUN-022) covers ministries, collectivities and sectoral networks together. The Taamir sources do not say how the municipal offices are connected; the institutional connection rests on separate sources (TUN-019, TUN-021), neither of which says how many municipal offices are on it, so the government-network flag is not set. Donor finance (TUN-005) is the Taamir platform's, not the connection's; TUN-016 and TUN-017 are from the excluded compilation and set nothing.

short: In 2025, 174 district councils worked in a national loans system and councils are on the government network; the share connected is not known.
gaps: No source gives a share of councils whose own offices are institutionally connected: the 174 district councils working in WEZESHA (TZA-006) come with no total and no statement of how the offices are connected, and GovNet's 265 connected bodies (TZA-015/016, February 2024) are not split between MDAs and LGAs. The newer connection fact (TZA-019, May 2026) reports staff buying their own bundles, but for Geita Region only, so it disagrees with TZA-015 without carrying the country; the newest authorities fact (TZA-002) is not-published, for e-Ardhi alone.

short: In 2022, 60.6 per cent of districts, municipalities and town councils answering a survey had office internet; the share of all is not known.
gaps: The 60.6% is a 2022 survey share of responding local governments (95 of 128 sampled districts, with 17 municipalities and 10 town councils), not of all of them, and no later share is published; the rural share is not given. The newer facts are counts with no total (61 sites in 2023, 20 districts in 2024, 13 in 2026) or concern sub-offices (25 lower local governments on SCART, Hoima's divisions), and the Vision's annex share of 74% is read from a flattened table reversed against its Table 1 (44% at 2020) and does not stand over the survey's. Finance for the connection inside the window is a Chinese loan for Phase V and unreleased World Bank funds (UGA-025, UGA-041); no domestic line for local governments is stated.

short: Municipalities across the Eastern Cape have worked in a shared disaster system since 2025; how many municipalities' offices are connected is not known.
gaps: No source gives a share or a count of municipalities connected against the national total; the one count is a single metro. How the offices working in the Eastern Cape disaster system and the rural Limpopo offices are connected is not stated, and the only institutional connection on record is one metro's network upgrade at its first phase with the last-mile provider not yet appointed. The governance values are that metro's own, its three-year plan's period is not given, and the AARTO fact does not say the integration is done at municipal offices.

short: Government counted 93 of 116 councils on its network in 2025 and all 116 in March 2026; the rural share is not known.
gaps: No figure gives the rural share, so the 116 of 116 that Smart Zambia stated in March 2026 cannot reach stage 5. That figure disagrees with later facts: Sinazongwe Town Council was reported as receiving its connection in August 2026 under a programme that still 'seeks to connect' all 116 councils, and North-Western Province's councils were announced connected in July 2026; the budget address of September 2025 counted 93 of 116. Use in a national system is not stated in so many words as done at the council office (the CDF system's data entry 'across councils', and a 2023 survey's e-procurement), and the financing is the plan's stated intention, not a budget line for council connections.

short: Government handed over 250 satellite kits for local authorities in 2025; whether any council office is connected is not known.
gaps: No row says a local authority's office is connected and in use: the 250 Starlink kits of July 2025 were handed over with installation still to come, the 104 Masvingo kits are one total for schools, clinics and local authorities with no council count and no statement that they are activated, and Manyame's connection is not said to be live. No plan naming the connection of local authorities is held, the domestic finance is one council's own budget (the national donation's finance is not stated), and no national count or share of councils connected is published.

short: A finance ministry system recording municipal payers and fees was put in all 164 municipalities by 2021; how many record in it is not known.
gaps: No share or count of municipalities whose staff record in the Portal do Munícipe: 164 of 164 is the ministry's figure for where it was implemented, with telecommunications problems in some. Nothing is dated after November 2021, so governance and the last twelve months hold nothing; the 2019 fact (AGO-009) read the Portal as receipts, the 2021 fact as a register.

short: Thirty communes collect local revenue electronically by 2026, recording payments only; where the record is held and the share of communes are not known.
gaps: No register of payers is described in any system, and where the electronic record is held is not stated: the only held fact is manual collection in 2021 (BDI-018), before the systems. The 30 communes carry no total; the only denominator in the evidence is 119 communes in 2021 (BDI-019), not dated to the count, so no share is taken. Owner disagrees: the ministry's budget line (BDI-004) and a bank's platform (BDI-012).

short: Twelve of 77 communes were selected in 2019 for cash-desk software that records payments; whether they were equipped and use it is not known.
gaps: Whether the 12 selected communes of 77 were equipped and went live is not established: the one source, of September 2019, says they were to be equipped during 2019/2020. Nothing is dated since, so governance and the last twelve months hold nothing; the partner ownership and donor finance of 2019 fall outside the 36 months.

The paper fact is one trader's account of Bangui in December 2020 and is not a statement about local governments at large; plan and finance are not stated.

short: A ministry-built register system was in a 22-commune pilot of 201 in December 2025; whether any commune records in it is not known.
gaps: No fact says SYGIDAN Recettes is live in any commune: it was at pre-validation in April 2024, and in December 2025 one commune was handed its taxpayer database within the pilot. Register and shared describe the design, not use; no count of communes recording is given. The costed plan (CIV-021) ran to June 2024 and is not current at the as-at, and no last-twelve-months fact is held.

short: Tools to track revenue and register taxpayers were being assessed with 20 decentralised territorial entities in 2024; whether any uses one is not known.
gaps: One fact only: a July 2024 workshop to standardise and assess tools for tracking revenue and registering taxpayers, with 20 entities in four provinces whose tier is not stated. What is recorded, where it is held, whether any entity uses a tool, the owner and any plan are not stated; the provincial systems in Kinshasa, Tshopo and Kasaï Central are upper-tier and place nothing.

short: A state platform for local governments' revenue was validated in February 2026; whether any local government yet records on it is not known.
gaps: No local government is stated as live on PDRCL: validated in February 2026, deployment 'imminent', one market pilot in Pointe-Noire 'to be deployed' after training. COG-009 (2026-04-30) describes transactions only, against the register of COG-002 and COG-013; no plan naming the system is stated.

short: Nothing is held on local governments' revenue records, digital or paper, and no system is named, so no stage is set.

gaps: No coverage fact is held: what is recorded, where it is held and how many municipalities record are not established. short: A central authority collects the real estate tax, a quarter for local government (2020); local records are not known, so no stage is set.

short: A revenue tool was presented in March 2025 for a pilot in communes of Conakry, Coyah and Kindia; whether the pilot began is not known.

gaps: The share is 60 of 432 principal centres on BUNEC's figures of 14 September 2026, which the source calls a pilot phase; the 2,400 or so secondary centres are outside the denominator and are planned to stay on paper, so the share of all local offices is lower and not published. Last twelve months disagree: EcoMatin says the rate has hardly moved since April 2022, while dated events show first digital birth acts at Limbe I on 7 January 2026 and in the East Region by August 2026. No national budget line is stated; one commune's maintenance line does not carry the country.

short: In August 2025 one commune of the capital was piloting digital civil registration; whether any birth or death has been registered digitally is not known.
gaps: No fact says an event has been registered digitally: the Masina pilot's births and deaths are stated as its aim (18 August 2025), and its own dates and results are not given. Last twelve months rests on a UNDP tender of 25 April 2026 for the design of digital tools; the one other dated event, a North Kivu sector office out of paper registers in July 2026, is one office and does not carry the country. No count of offices newer than the 979 of March 2019.

short: A civil registration system was built and validated by September 2026 but no office uses it; whether older urban systems still run is not known.
gaps: No office is said to use SIFEC at 22 September 2026, and the B;D rows (COG-004, 006, 008, 018, 022) give the scope of a system not yet deployed, so events is read as none. Older facts disagree with the newest: electronic records kept locally in some Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire centres (COG-032, 2021; COG-036 and 2 of Brazzaville's 10 offices digitised, COG-037, 2020) against a system called manual in 2026 (COG-017) and 2024 (COG-043); nothing since 2021 says whether those urban systems still run. Finance: COG-015 (not stated, for SIFEC's deployment) is newer than the donor rows COG-030 and COG-025. The roadmap (COG-034, COG-039) is from 2020-21 with no period given; the plan held is the national civil-status reform policy for 2022-2026 (COG-044), whose period includes the as-at.

short: In 2026 offices register on paper while a digital system is studied and costed; when its three-centre pilot starts is not known.
gaps: No system exists yet: the eCRVS is proposed by a study validated on 25 March 2026, and its three-centre pilot (Moroni, Mutsamudu, Fomboni) has not started. The costed plan (COM-004) and the 2024 strategic plan (COM-022) are given no period; plan:current rests on COM-004 saying the country holds it in August 2026. The newest paper statements say 'largely' paper (COM-001, COM-021), not paper only; the only flat statement is from 2017 (COM-034). COM-016 (ANEC decree not adopted, March 2026) is the one no-change event against nine advancing.

short: In 2017 offices in all 22 municipalities entered births and deaths digitally, in urban centres only; whether records reach the national register is not known.
gaps: No report of practice says the entry made at the conservatória is held in the national register: CPV-008 (2017) does not say where the record is held, CPV-001 (2025) does not say the entry is made at the office, and CPV-003 and CPV-005 are what the law prescribes, which places nothing. The office share is 22 of 22 municipalities from a profile compiled to November 2017, with stations in urban centres only; nothing newer gives a share or a rural share. No governance fact is dated inside the 36 months and no event inside the twelve.

short: Nine civil-status sites in Djibouti-Ville have entered births and deaths digitally since 2011, as stated in 2024; digital entry outside the capital is not known.
gaps: The newest dated facts (ESCWA's 2025 survey, DJI-003 to DJI-005, held as an ingest note and not as the passage) say local offices hold no electronic records of births or deaths, which disagrees with the city's 2024 account of SIGEC; no row dated to the as-at says any office outside Djibouti-Ville enters digitally, none gives a national count of offices, and SIGEC is not said to be held in a national register. No plan is stated, nothing is held for the last twelve months, and no row shows a birth registration issuing the NNI in practice, so identity integrated is not set; no admissible row names rural offices, so rural gap is not set.

short: Births are registered in a national digital register across 1,541 communes, a 2019 count; the share of local offices entering digitally is not known.
gaps: The 1,541 commune databases are a 2019 count given with no total of local offices (communes and their administrative annexes), and the newest offices fact (DZA-012, 2025) gives no count or share entering digitally and finds paper persisting. The facts valued connected (DZA-002, DZA-008) do not say the entry is made at the commune office when the event is registered; the law keeps paper registers and sends a digitised copy. Nothing is held for the last twelve months and no rural figure is given.

short: Births and deaths are entered digitally at 4,571 health offices, as stated in 2026; the share of all offices is not known.
gaps: No total of health offices is given against the 4,571 (2017 and 2026) or the 4,666 linked (2025), and the two counts differ; 'full nationwide automation' is a statement of offices automated, not a share registering. Egypt's undated answers to the WHO EMRO questionnaire (published 2025) disagree: paper at registration points, electronic entry at the governorate centre, and health-office entry only as a pilot in selected governorates. Finance is not stated in the newest fact, though a 2024 page credits the State budget; no rural share is published.

short: Births and deaths were handwritten at local offices and entered in regional electronic registers one level up in 2017; current practice is not known.
gaps: The record-making facts date from 2015 and 2017 and nothing since describes how a birth is entered; the newest events fact (ERI-006, 2025-11) names only the computerised death certificate and does not say where it is entered, so B rests on ERI-009. No count of offices doing digital entry, no owner and no finance are stated, the 2024-2028 plan is not said to name a digital system, and nothing is held for the last twelve months.

short: Digital registration of births and deaths is in pilot, in Addis Ababa and 1,300 of 19,202 kebeles in 2025; use beyond pilots is not known.
gaps: No fact shows a system past its pilot outside Addis Ababa: the July 2026 presentation does not say which rollout phase had been reached, and the offices facts disagree (pilot in ETH-003, ETH-011, ETH-016 and ETH-023; count:50 in ETH-013, an announced start in the capital with no total; count:100 in ETH-027, capital only, 2018). The connected facts do not say the entry is made at the office, and ETH-015 (2025-07) calls registration mainly paper-based. Finance is not stated for the eCRVS, and the only finance fact in the window is donor support to ME-CRVS (ETH-025, 2023). Whether the birth feeds the Fayda number is stated only as a possibility in systems.csv, so identity integrated is not set.

short: No office registered births or deaths digitally in May 2026; a system is being prepared with funding to 2028; its first offices are not known.
gaps: No office registers digitally and no pilot office is named; the CNEC is not yet in operation and the legal framework for digital registration was rated not implemented at 31 May 2026. The count held is of departments (0 of an unstated total), not offices. No domestic budget line is stated. GAB-001 and GAB-002 are dated after the as-at and set nothing.

short: Births were registered digitally at two Accra registry centres in 2024; how many offices do so, and how the record is made, is not known.
gaps: No national count or share of offices entering births digitally: the only count is two registry centres in one Accra municipal district (2024-10), a floor. How a birth record is made is not stated in any row; the one `made` fact is for deaths, paper forms scanned at the national office (2022), and nothing says entry is made at the office and held in the national register. Deaths rest on the platform's name and on scanned forms. No dated event in the twelve months. The plan for 2025-2030 was still to be approved in July 2025 and does not name the platform; the budget line names no system. The identity link was launched in March 2024 and systems.csv records it suspended after a fault and re-tested in August 2026. GHA-002 to GHA-004 are from the excluded source and set nothing.

short: Commune offices made digital birth certificates in September 2026, when a paper shortage halted printing; how many offices do so is not known.
gaps: No count or share of offices: one commune's officer says all communes, with no count beside it, so it is not read as 100 per cent. `made` disagrees: GIN-002 (2026-09-02) has the commune system depending on a data centre, while GIN-010 (2026-03-03) has Conakry's 13 communes supplied with paper registers for 2026 and GIN-018 (2026-02) has registrars still on paper in parallel; the newest stands, but its words do not say the entry is made at the office. Offices disagree too: pilot in ten communes (GIN-013, 2023-08) against not-published (GIN-003), the newest standing. The fact does not say whether the digital birth certificate is the registration of the birth or the issue of a secure copy, nor whether the system is E-RENEC. No plan is stated. Owner disagrees in the window: vendor (2026-09), partner (2026-04), ministry in law (2025-04, 2023-10). GIN-017 (July 2025) falls outside the twelve months. GIN-006 to GIN-009 are from the excluded source and set nothing.

short: Births are registered on a central digital system, with 79 local offices holding digital registers in 2025; the total number of offices is not known.
gaps: The 79 civil registration offices have no total against them, so the count is a floor; the same 2025 source also yields 258 health facility points (GMB-016) and, in its deck, no figure for how many points enter records (GMB-035). Both `connected` facts say the source does not state in terms that the record is keyed at the registration point at the moment of registration. No death module is in operation. GMB-021 and GMB-022 (a policy published 2024-02) call CRVS paper-based with no event registered digitally; the newer facts stand. No domestic budget line is stated and the World Bank operation ended in August 2025. The CRVS strategy was still to be finalised in the 2025 diagnostic; plan:current rests on the 2023-2028 strategy and the 2021-2030 health policy. Backlog capture rests on one systems.csv line from the 2024 policy, undated in its text. GMB-036 (April 2025) falls outside the twelve months. GMB-006 and GMB-007 are from the excluded source and set nothing.

short: One Bissau office registers births and deaths digitally in 2026, and health posts in three regions register births; the share of offices is not known.
gaps: No count of offices or posts entering digitally against the country's own total (13 conservatórias and 80 posts in GNB-030; 55 offices and 20 health sites in GNB-035): the one counted office, Santa Luzia, is in Bissau, and the posts in Tombali and Quinara (GNB-011, GNB-012) are uncounted, on a platform the source does not name or say is connected. GNB-007 calls Santa Luzia the first fully digital office in 2026 while GNB-011 and GNB-015 report digital registration from 2025; no dated source in the evidence other than the excluded essay says rural offices are outside the system, so rural gap is not set.

short: A digital pilot registers births in Malabo only, since 2018, and the seven regional offices use paper in 2024; its present state is not known.
gaps: Nothing on the state of SIREC is dated after the World Bank diagnostic of 2024, and nothing falls in the twelve months to the as-at. No fact says how the pilot itself makes the record, or how many offices in Malabo use it. Every owner fact is dated 2017 or 2018, outside the 36 months, so owner is left empty; the plan held (GNQ-010, 2022-2026) is the statistics strategy and its passages do not say what the civil registry system does.

short: More than 270,000 births were registered digitally from hospitals in two months of 2026; how many offices or hospitals use the system is not known.
gaps: No fact counts the hospitals or offices using the e-birth registry of 2026; the newest offices fact, KEN-014 for 2023, reports no office entering digitally, and predates the system. KEN-002 has parents entering the data in the hospital and does not say the entry is made at a registration office; systems.csv carries the same system as an e-notification processed at the civil registration office. Deaths are not on the system. No plan is held for the period: KEN-023's ran 2018 to 2022.

short: County teams registered births online in 2024, with deaths added to the platform; how many of the 58 centres enter them is not known.
gaps: No source counts the centres entering births on the DHIS2 platform: the two newest office facts (LBR-012, LBR-015; 15 counties, 58 centres) publish no number, and the only count is 14 centres in 2015 with no total (LBR-032), which does not say the centres make the digital entry. LBR-017 (May 2024) says County Service Center services remain mostly paper, against LBR-010's county teams registering online; the 2024 policy (LBR-006) gives no period and is not said to name the platform; nothing is dated inside the twelve months, the last event being 2024 (LBR-013).

short: All civil registration offices were automated and linked to one database, the health ministry said in 2022; whether events are entered there is not known.
gaps: LBY-006 and LBY-007 say all offices are fully automated and electronically linked to one database; they do not say a birth or death is entered at the office when it is registered, so the share is read as equipped, not registering. The figure is the health ministry's, undated and published 2022, with two counts of service offices (400 and 380) and no rural share; no plan or finance is stated in the 36 months.

short: Births were registered digitally at 30 health-facility stations in three districts in 2026; the total number of local offices is not known.
gaps: No total of local registration offices is given, so both counts are floors: 30 SMS-supported stations in three districts (LSO-002, 2026) and 15 enrolment centres online to the central server (LSO-023, 2022), which are different systems and are not reconciled. How the SMS platform's record is made and where it is held is not stated, LSO-014 does not name the register, and LSO-022 says the centres allow for birth registration without saying the entry is made there; nationwide scale-up is an action for 2026-2027 and deaths are not shown entered at any local office.

short: Offices enter births and deaths in a ministry system said in 2024 to reach every office; the share of offices registering digitally is not known.
gaps: No share of offices registering is held: 'all offices' (MAR-013, 2024-10-29) is the ministry's word with no count beside it, and the 59 of 97 (MAR-004, 2026-01-30) is over a programme's participating municipalities for a system whose function the report does not state. Later facts disagree with the 2024 account: in October 2025 communes were short of the paper registers called essential for registering births (MAR-009) and access to the national platform was still to be opened (MAR-010); MAR-014 gives the central connected platform as what the programme is to provide. The plan (MAR-016) carries no period, the domestic finance fact is from 2014 and outside the window, and the identifier at birth is held only as what Law 36-21 provides.

short: Communes register births digitally, 336 of them in December 2025; the share of all communes this represents is not known.
gaps: The 336 communes (MDG-007, December 2025) are given as 40% of the project's target, not as a share of all communes, so the count is a floor; the newer fact (MDG-005, 2026-03-02) says only 'several communes'. MDG-009 does not say in terms where the record is held, and the offline module was only in demonstration. The plan held is the national decentralisation plan to 2030, which carries digital civil-status centres as an indicator (MDG-042); no domestic budget line is held, and PRODIGY's financing closed on 30 June 2026 with no later fact on what funds the system; the software's future after OpenCRVS stops was unsettled. No digital death registration is reported.

short: Births were registered on paper in July 2026 and a digital platform had ten pilot areas named; whether any has started is not known.
gaps: No office is shown entering an event digitally: the platform of MLI-007 and MLI-008 (2024-12-16) is approved with ten pilot areas identified and not said to have started, so B;D is what it is to cover, not what is registered. Nothing dated inside the twelve months speaks to movement. The strategy held is for 2018-2022 (MLI-014), a period ended before the as-at, so no current plan is held; finance:domestic rests on ANSAEC's endowment in law with no amount or budget line (MLI-005), beside donor support (MLI-009). The 2016 City-web fact (MLI-011) names no office and its link to the NINA is not confirmed at the as-at, so identity integrated is not set.

short: Births are entered directly at district offices and all 68 conservatories were digitised by 2025; the share of local offices entering digitally is not known.
gaps: No share or count with a denominator of local offices making the digital entry: the registrar's 68 of 68 conservatories are 'digitised' (equipped) and leave out the posts below them, and the newest fact (MOZ-006, 2026-08-28) publishes no figure. Facts disagree on deaths (MOZ-004 and MOZ-033 give B and D; MOZ-016, 2025, names death registration as a challenge) and on how the record is made (MOZ-034 has district offices entering directly; MOZ-035 has 534 community points on paper forms keyed at the district office, which no fact calls rural, so no rural gap is flagged); MOZ-001 does not say the new maternity posts enter digitally.

short: By law births are recorded centrally at citizen reception centres, 153 of 168 equipped in 2021; whether centres enter births digitally is not known.
gaps: No fact outside the law says a centre enters a birth digitally when it is declared: events and how the record is made rest on Laws 2011-003 and 2025-011 (MRT-003, MRT-004, MRT-009, MRT-010), which place nothing, and the one other fact on either is from the excluded essay. The office figure is centres equipped against a planned network of 168, from August 2021, with nothing newer; no governance fact falls inside the 36 months (the newest is 2022-11) and nothing is held for the last twelve months.

short: Births and deaths are registered online at computerised civil status offices, 35 listed in 2019; the share of all offices is not known.
gaps: No share of offices making the digital entry: the Registrar's 35 computerised offices (2019) is a count with no denominator, the deck does not say in terms that every office enters records, and the newest fact (MUS-007, 2025-09-06) gives no count; the only share, 32 of 47 in 2012, is from the excluded essay. The plan held (MUS-018) is the Strategic Directions for 2023/2024, a period ended before the as-at, and both last-twelve-months facts (MUS-005 of 2025-09-06, MUS-020 of 2024) fall before the window opens on 2025-09-30.

short: Births and deaths were entered digitally at 87 local service points in five districts in 2025; the share of local offices is not known.
gaps: No share of local offices is published: 87 Traditional Authority service points in five of 28 districts stand against 277 TAs and 138 Sub-TAs listed for expansion, and the 58 health facilities (2025) and 142 health centres (plan) carry no total. MWI-039 (owner:partner, CDC and EGPAF maintaining the CRVS system) disagrees with the newer owner:ministry rows; MWI-033 records CDC funding expected to stop in March 2026, an expectation and not an event; the NRB's own 2025 pages (MWI-049, MWI-052) describe a paper NR8 procedure and name no digital system; the rural gap rests on MWI-044 (2024), which gives no figure. MWI-001 to MWI-003 are dated after the as-at and MWI-007 to MWI-011 are from an excluded source: none was used.

short: Local offices enter births and deaths in the national register, as reported in 2024; the share of offices doing so is not known.
gaps: No share of offices registering digitally stands at the as-at. The newest office fact, NAM-014 (statistics agency, April 2024), says some remote offices lack computers or internet and gives no count; it disagrees with NAM-025 (September 2023, share:100%), which says all 62 local centres are connected to the NPRS, is not the registrar's or the statistics office's statement, lists offices that sum to 59, and is contradicted in the same document by NAM-026. No plan covering the as-at is held: the CRVS plan ran 2015/16 to 2020/21 and no later one is named. finance:domestic rests on NAM-020, dated at the window's first day. The rural gap carries no figure, and backlog capture rests on systems.csv (a running project to capture old death records, 2023). NAM-001 to NAM-003 and NAM-040 to NAM-044 are from excluded sources and were not used.

short: The digital register ran in 101 of 266 communes in December 2024, a share of communes; digital death registration outside Niamey is not known.
gaps: The share is 100 communes of 266 principal centres (NER-033, an undated page given the year 2026), a share of communes read as offices; it agrees with the statistics office's 101 of 266 in production (NER-042, December 2024) and the government's 102 communes with no total (NER-027, April 2026). It disagrees with NER-014 (UNICEF, 10 August 2026), 68 per cent of communes computerised with no numerator or denominator, which is a share equipped and would also place at stage 3. Deaths are evidenced digitally only for the five Niamey arrondissements in 2023 (NER-046); NER-040 and NER-041 (December 2024) call registration paper based, against the connected rows. The 13,939 village and health-facility declaration centres are not said to be computerised, and the rural gap rests on NER-049 (2023), with no figure. Most last-twelve-month rows are works announced, not delivered, and the commune count did not rise between May 2025 (103) and April 2026 (102). NER-031 and NER-032 are from an excluded source and were not used.

short: Births and deaths are entered digitally at ward and local government offices from July 2026; the share of local offices doing so is not known.
gaps: No share of local offices entering on VitalReg is established: 3,372 wards activated (NGA-027, 18 July 2026) has no total of wards, and the 4,011 registration centres (NGA-014, NGA-023, NGA-035) are a count of centres whose facts say they do not state how many enter on the platform; the two counts disagree and are of different units. NGA-027 also says only 15 states have ward registrars while other rows say all 36 states and the FCT, and paper fallback where the network fails is reported (NGA-001, NGA-040, NGA-041). Finance is donor or not stated; no domestic budget line is held.

short: Births and deaths are entered digitally at all categories of registration office in 2025, the statistics office says; the rural share is not known.
gaps: The 100 per cent is the statistics institute's statement that NCI-CRVS is fully operational at all categories of registration office in 2025, beside the totals of 416 sectors and 2,148 cells; it gives no count of offices using the system and no rural share. The two newer offices rows (RWA-002, RWA-006) publish no figure, and RWA-006 has cell secretaries still in training, in a text dated by publication that reads as older. Within the twelve months RWA-024 reports timely death registration falling from 96.3% to 89.9% in 2025, against rising completeness (RWA-023); the launches in RWA-009 and RWA-016 carry publication dates only.

short: Births are registered in a national electronic registry, with one local office named in 2026; how many offices enter records, and where, is not known.
gaps: How the record is made rests on a 2023 account of the pre-war centralised electronic registry (SDN-010), which does not say at which desk the birth entry is keyed; nothing since the war began says how or where the record is made. The only office figure is one office issuing an electronic birth certificate on 17 May 2026 (SDN-005), with no total and no statement of how the underlying record is made. The twelve months disagree: closures in Darfur and Khartoum (SDN-001, SDN-002) are undated and carry publication dates, while the dated events are two Gezira offices reopening (SDN-004, SDN-006), so no flag is set. No governance fact falls inside the 36 months; deaths are not evidenced.

short: In 2026 civil-status centres register births in one national system, with 77% of 629 centres digitised; the share entering data is not known.
gaps: No fact gives a share or count of centres registering events in the LGEC: every figure (77% of 629 in September 2026, 471 and 437 of 629 earlier) is centres digitised, deployed or covered, and SEN-015 itself says equipped centres are not the same as centres entering data. Deaths are held in the system (SEN-034) but no fact says they are entered at the office at registration; no rural share is given, only regional deployment rates (SEN-032); the total of centres is 629 in 2026 and 689 in SEN-054; finance:domestic rests on an unnotified 2026 agency budget (SEN-013) and an unquantified 'substantial public funding' (SEN-056), beside EU finance to June 2026 (SEN-042).

short: In 2023 births were entered digitally at the registration authority's hospital centres and sent to a central registry; the number of offices is not known.
gaps: No count or share of offices doing the digital entry is published: the 48 (SLE-018, September 2024) are health facilities given laptops and modems, none said to be registering, so the count is a floor of equipped sites at best. The only offices named as entering births digitally are in Freetown (Ola During Hospital, 34 Military Hospital), the fact for entry at the office dates from March 2023, and death registration with the application is not described. No plan with a period covering the as-at is held (the 2017 roadmap gives none), no domestic budget line appears in an evidence row inside 36 months, and nothing is dated inside the last twelve months.

short: By January 2026 local administrations in 30 districts registered births digitally into one central database; the total of districts or offices is not known.
gaps: The 30 districts (SOM-008) carry no total of districts or offices, so the count is a floor and no share can be read; it is a count of districts read as offices, on an undated page whose January 2026 date is a proxy. Deaths are enabled on the platform (SOM-010) but only births are counted as registered (SOM-007). SOM-012 calls the 19 districts of August 2025 a pilot where SOM-009 calls the system production-level; the newer stands. No dated event falls inside the last twelve months: the launch of 10 August 2025 (SOM-016) is outside it, and the move from 19 to 30 districts has no date of its own. The roadmap (SOM-014) gives no period and no domestic budget line is stated.

short: A digital civil registration system was announced in July 2026 and no birth is registered digitally; its design and start date are not known.
gaps: Preparation rests on announcements of July 2026 and an undated memorandum of understanding: no design, procurement, pilot office or start date for a digital system is described, and whether the Juba birth-registration pilot (SSD-023, SSD-024) is digital is not stated. No dated statement that local offices register on paper only is held outside the excluded source (SSD-019), so stage 1 is not claimed. On the plan, SSD-022 (December 2025) says a costed CRVS plan was adopted but gives it no period, against SSD-013 (July 2026), which describes recommendations and no plan in force.

short: Births are entered directly in the national database at maternities, as of 2026; the share of local offices doing so is not known.
gaps: No share or count of local offices entering records is published: the registrar says all maternities, with no number and nothing on the other offices (STP-006), and the World Bank gives 11 centres and seven maternity posts without saying how many enter records in SIGA (STP-020). STP-019 (2022) says births of 2010 to 2023 sit on paper still to be digitised, against the connected entry of STP-005 and STP-018. Deaths are named for the system (STP-009, STP-010, STP-013) but no fact says where they are entered, and the newest fact (STP-004) names births only. No finance fact falls inside the 36 months; the plan named in STP-015 has no period and STP-022 says there is none for civil registration.

short: Births and deaths were entered in the national register at 14 service centres in 2022; the total number of offices is not known.
gaps: The 14 service centres registering in the National Population Register in 2022 (SWZ-012) come with no total of offices, so the count is a floor; the software 'installed in all centres' is equipped, not registering, and the AfDB and COMESA 'all offices' (SWZ-016) carries no count. The only total held is in a governance row of December 2024 (SWZ-015: 15 service centres including headquarters, and 5 hospital points), a different year and not read against the count. The World Bank's June 2026 appraisal disagrees with the older facts: well over 90% of civil records on paper (SWZ-001) and electronic civil registry services not active (SWZ-004). No rural share and no office figure within two years.

short: A computerised record of vital events was kept beside the manual register in 2018; where it is entered is not known.
gaps: No admitted fact says where the computerised Civil Status record is entered, at the offices at Praslin, La Digue and Anse Royale or centrally, nor how many local offices enter it; the only rows on `made` and `offices` (SYC-001, SYC-002) are from the excluded source. The one placing fact is dated 2018-08-10, and nothing on governance or the last twelve months falls inside the windows: SYC-004 to SYC-006 (owner:ministry, latest 2022-11-01) are older than 36 months and are not carried.

short: Births were registered digitally at 97 hospital registry points in 2025; the total of local offices is not known.
gaps: The 97 digitised hospital-based registration points (TCD-016) have no total of local offices beside them, so the count is a floor and no share is established; deaths are not registered digitally on any fact. `made` disagrees: N'Djamena's commune service is still described as paper on 2026-09-23 (TCD-001, TCD-004) and the national system as predominantly paper in 2024 (TCD-019), while the hospital offices are connected (TCD-017, TCD-044); the commune facts are one municipality and do not carry the country. TCD-017's words do not say the entry is made at the office, which only TCD-044 says, of six hospitals in 2023. No admitted source states a rural gap, and the N'Djamena register digitisation is planned, not under way.

short: A digital birth registration platform was piloted at one town hall in 2024; whether other offices register on it is not known.
gaps: No admitted fact says how the record is made on the digital birth registration platform or on Kadodo: the only `made` row, TGO-015, is 2018 data and speaks of paper exchange between offices, not of the entry. The 16 Savanes communes (TGO-010) are centres digitised and trained to use the platform, not said to register on it, and no total is given beside them (TGO-001 mentions 117 communes). Events disagree: the 2024 platform names births only (TGO-008), Kadodo in Lacs 1 named births and deaths in 2021 (TGO-012). The owner is now held from the July 2026 tender (TGO-016), which names the digital ministry as employer of a sixteen-commune pilot financed by a German development bank; the 2024 roadmap (TGO-006) gives no period.

short: Registrars enter births and deaths into the national database after the paper register, all offices connected in 2020; how many register is not known.
gaps: No source gives a share or count of offices making the entry in Madania: TUN-018 (2020) and TUN-012 (2015) say all offices are interconnected or have access and give no number registering. Nothing on how the record is made or on offices is dated after 2020; no plan whose period includes the as-at and no finance fact inside the 36 months is held (TUN-009 and TUN-020 plans ended by 2021, TUN-019 donor finance is 2021).

short: In 2024 57% of mainland registration centres were active, entering births by phone; capped because a current plan or domestic finance is not known.
gaps: Staged on the mainland (RITA); Zanzibar's eCRVS runs in all 11 districts with no count of offices (TZA-003), and a 2025 paper calls it primarily paper-based (TZA-007). The 57% is centres RITA counts as active, the inactive ones lacking the phone that uploads, not a stated count of centres entering digitally; TZA-017 says some centres' registrations are keyed by district officers, and the newer TZA-011 (12,025 points, 2025) gives no total and no number entering digitally. Inside the 36 months no domestic finance fact is held (TZA-025 is 2018) and the plan in TZA-014 ran to 2025/26, ending June 2026; the only event inside the twelve months is Zanzibar's (TZA-005), the mainland's being October 2024.

short: District offices enter births and deaths into the central register, in most districts in 2020; how many offices do so is not known.
gaps: No share or count of offices making the entry is held: UGA-034 (2020) gives MVRS as used in 112 of 135 districts, and 122 elsewhere in the same brief, and nothing on offices or on how the record is made is dated after 2020. The sources disagree on how the record is made: NIRA's January 2019 questionnaire has paper at the lowest centres keyed at regional level (UGA-040), the 2020 brief has entry at district offices into the central register (UGA-033). UGA-002 (July 2026) reports a new births module on NSIS with no offices and no date of going live, and UGA-009 does not say the current plan names a registration system; no dated event falls inside the twelve months.

short: Births are registered online at 242 equipped health facilities, as of March 2026; the share of local offices registering digitally is not known.
gaps: No share of local offices registering digitally is published: 242 health facilities are counted as equipped (ZAF-010, March 2026) against no total, the health department counts 299 of 1,445 maternity facilities (ZAF-040, March 2025) and an older count gives 391, and how the 325 front offices make the record is stated only in general terms (ZAF-021). Deaths have no digital registration on record; the twelve-month advance (ZAF-046) carries no figure, while e-Birth missed its 2025/26 targets (ZAF-047, ZAF-051); no dated source says in terms that rural offices are outside the system, so rural gap is not set. ZAF-001 and ZAF-002 are dated after the as-at and ZAF-006 to ZAF-008 are from an excluded source; none was used.

short: Births are registered in a national system deployed in eleven districts in 2026; how many local offices enter records themselves is not known.
gaps: No count of local offices that enter events in INRIS themselves is published, and the figures disagree: the Minister's 2026 statement has INRIS deployed in eleven districts with no total (ZMB-006), a 2025 case study has access in 81 of 116 districts (ZMB-020), and earlier accounts give 26 district offices and over 40 districts; each is deployment or access, not offices registering. The facts also disagree on where entry is made: ZMB-015 and ZMB-017 have paper forms keyed at provincial or national headquarters, while ZMB-002 has one district office registering through INRIS in September 2026, which does not carry the country. Deaths are reported registered in INRIS (ZMB-010, ZMB-016), though the Minister names death certificates only as intended (ZMB-007). The cost of the exercise is stated without a source of funds (ZMB-009), an older fact naming donors (ZMB-022). Nothing dated inside the twelve months says the system advanced or regressed nationally. ZMB-004 and ZMB-005 are from an excluded source.

short: Births are entered digitally at computerised offices; at least 93 of 282 offices were computerised in 2026, and how many register digitally is not known.
gaps: The Registrar General's department counts all 10 provincial and 63 district offices and more than 20 of 209 sub-offices as computerised (ZWE-010), at least 93 of 282, and does not say what a computerised office does: that is a share equipped, about 33 per cent, not a share registering. ZWE-020 says entry is made in real time at the office but not where the record is held or whether offices are online to a national register; some sub-offices are still not computerised (ZWE-003, ZWE-007). Deaths have no digital entry on record. Finance for the computerisation is donor in every fact that names it, while the 2026 Appropriation Act funds the civil registration programme whole from domestic revenue with no system line (ZWE-014). The February 2026 shortage of certificate paper (ZWE-013) is a regress in issuing certificates, not in digital entry, and is not flagged. ZWE-012 is from an excluded source.

short: Schools answered a twice-yearly school count questionnaire in 2021/22; whether any primary school keeps a per-pupil record is not known, so no stage is set.
gaps: The only evidence row, AGO-001, is from the source the study excludes and sets nothing. No admissible dated statement that primary schools keep learner records on paper, and no admissible fact on any system holding a record per learner; systems.csv holds only census-class and unclassified systems.

short: In 2023 the yearly school count was collected on paper; whether primary schools keep per-pupil records is not known, so no stage is set.
gaps: The only evidence row, BDI-001, is from the source the study excludes and sets nothing. No admissible dated statement that primary schools keep learner records on paper, and no admissible fact on any system holding a record per learner; systems.csv holds only census, single-function, learning, enabling and unclassified systems.

short: Primary schools entered enrolments and class lists themselves in 2026; how many do, and whether any enter attendance or results, is not known.
gaps: No count or share of primary schools entering data is published; the minister's letter of 16 February 2026 says only that several schools update the CEP class alone. No fact shows primary schools entering attendance or results: the kept facts disagree, the newest (BEN-005, BEN-002) giving enrolment and the routine entry of BEN-011 being secondary only, with BEN-015 of 2020 not saying how often or at which level results are entered. Finance is not stated, and the plan held (BEN-017) ended in 2021 and is not current. BEN-003 is from the excluded source and sets nothing.

short: A national pupil register was in pilot in 2024 and enrolment had not begun by June 2025; the number of schools is not known.
gaps: No source gives a count of pilot establishments or says whether they are primary or secondary, and none reports FIUE-BF or the national pupil file past its pilot: at 25 June 2025 enrolment had not begun and at 14 April 2025 the student management platform was still to be designed. The sources disagree on how the record is kept (BFA-017 pilot establishments online in 2023, BFA-009 mainly hard copies in April 2025) and BFA-017 does not say results are entered during the year; finance was the general budget in February 2024 (BFA-014) and donor only in the newer rows; no current plan naming the system and no dated event in the twelve months are held.

short: A fund was connecting remote primary schools to broadband in 2024; how schools keep pupil records is not known, so no stage is set.
gaps: The one evidence row (BWA-001, records on paper) is from the excluded source and sets nothing, so no admissible dated statement of absence is held. The systems on file are noted classes only: an annual school census called EMIS, one standalone attendance tablet in a single school, and school connectivity; the 2025 EMIS/LMS tenders are named without a class.

short: By 2026 the ministry ran a yearly school count; whether schools keep a per-pupil record is not known, so no stage is set.
gaps: The one evidence row (CAF-001, paper registers) is from the excluded source and sets nothing, so no admissible dated statement of absence is held. The systems on file are noted classes only: the SIGE/EMIS as an annual school census with its statistical yearbook, and single-function systems for teachers (HRMIS, ESIGAPE, EduTrac) and learning assessment; no system holding a record per learner is described.

short: A per-pupil performance record started in five Abidjan pilot schools, level not named, in January 2024; whether it went further is not known.
gaps: Nothing shows DOBCONNECT past its 5 pilot establishments of January 2024, whose level is not stated and is read as primary; the May 2024 rollout is given only as planned, and who enters the data is not said. SMART ECOLE (2019) gives no schools using it, and its record is pupils identifying themselves online (kept disagrees: enrolment against DOBCONNECT's routine). Owner is held only from 2019, outside the 36 months; finance not stated; nothing in the last twelve months.

short: How primary schools keep their pupils' records is not known, so no stage is set.
gaps: The one evidence row (CMR-001, paper registers) is from the source the study excludes and sets nothing. No admissible row says how primary schools keep learner records; systems.csv holds only a census platform (STATEDUC), an enabling pilot and three systems (SIGE, WebSIG, the integrated EMIS platform) with no class and no described function.

short: Ministry staff, not schools, registered pupils by app in a 20-primary-school pilot in April 2026; whether it will go national is not known.
gaps: EDUSER is established only as a three-week pilot in 20 primary schools of one province (April 2026), with SERNIE staff, not the schools, doing the entry; a national rollout is unfunded and no plan naming the system is held. No national count or share of schools; COD-008 and COD-009 are from the excluded source and set nothing.

short: A November 2023 decree creates a per-pupil record that schools are to fill; whether any school uses it is not known.
gaps: Nothing shows staff trained, equipment delivered or any pilot school: the September 2023 ENT trial was only proposed, and no fact is dated after the decree of 2 November 2023. How the record is kept and the last twelve months are not held; the May 2023 statement of no plan falls outside the 36 months and is not carried.

short: Schools have entered marks since June 2025, and 45% of public primary schools were integrated by February 2026; the share entering marks is not known.
gaps: The 45% is a rate of integration of public primary schools at 2 February 2026, with no numerator or denominator, and not a share entering marks; private primary schools are not split out. ANADEN's June 2025 entry calls e-Msomo a pilot, which the later registration by island supersedes; no source says the plan names e-Msomo, and the only finance stated is UNICEF's. The rural statement in COM-001 is from the excluded source and sets nothing.

short: Teachers must record pupils' absences and marks in a system put in all 395 basic schools by 2019; the share entering them is not known.
gaps: No share or count of basic education schools entering attendance or marks is published: 395 of 395 (February 2019) is schools where SIGE was implemented, 'used in all' (June 2025) gives no count, and the compact's indicator of schools with a functional SIGE has no baseline. The newest fact, the despacho in force from 1 September 2025, gives no figure and states an obligation, not practice. Nothing is dated inside the last twelve months; the donor finance stated is for one module only.

short: In 2023 school heads registered pupils and sent absences through a national per-pupil record; the share of primary schools doing so is not known.
gaps: No share or count with a total of primary schools entering absences in GOSE: DJI-012 says all public schools transmit through it but gives no figure, and the project's own indicator on schools transmitting on time still read 'No' at 28 November 2023. The newest coverage facts are from 2023; DJI-006 (2019, none) disagrees with DJI-012 and is the older. No dated event in the twelve months to the as-at, no rural figure, and plan:current rests on a circular for the 2025-2026 school year, not a costed plan.

short: It is not known whether primary schools keep pupil records on paper or in a system, so no stage is set.
gaps: The one evidence row, DZA-001, is from the source the study excludes and sets nothing, so no aspect is held. Nothing admissible says whether primary schools keep learner records on paper or in a system, at which levels, or in how many schools.

short: The ministry's 2023-2027 plan is to build a per-pupil record; whether primary schools use one is not known, so no stage is set.

EGY-001 is from the excluded source and sets nothing; finance is not stated; owner:ministry is dated September 2023, at the edge of the 36-month window; no dated event in the twelve months to the as-at.

short: A digital platform for the yearly school count was built by 2026; how schools keep pupils' records is not known, so no stage is set.
gaps: The only evidence row, ERI-001, is from the excluded source and sets nothing. No admissible dated statement that primary schools keep learner records on paper, and no row on any system holding a record per learner.

short: The ministry's web-based system, with a number for each pupil, was piloted by June 2025; whether any primary school uses it is not known.

The plan held, ESDP VI, ran to 2024/25 and is not current at the as-at; no domestic finance is stated.

short: 728 schools managed pupils' marks in a vendor's application in 2024; the share of primary schools is not known, as no total is given.
gaps: The 728 schools are the press's and the vendor's count of schools using Xgest, with no level named (read as primary) and no total, so no share. `kept` disagrees: marks and results in Xgest at 27 September 2024 (GAB-015) against the ministry's order of 24 September 2024 that no personal data pass through it (GAB-017) and the once-a-year learner identification of 2025/2026 (GAB-010), which does not say whether school or family makes the entry. No count of schools in the SOSUP register; plan and finance not stated; Xgest itself is vendor-owned (GAB-016).

short: In November 2025, 733 primary schools reported each pupil's literacy and numeracy results on a digital platform; their share of primary schools is not known.
gaps: No total of primary schools is given beside the 733 reporting on the DL+ Platform, so no share can be read; the source does not say how often a school reports, and the platform's owner and any plan naming it are not stated. The count stood unchanged from August 2024 to November 2025. GHA-001 is from the excluded source and sets nothing.

short: In March 2026 a nationwide registration gave primary pupils a single school number, in secondary since 2022; how many schools took part is not known.
gaps: No number or share of primary schools registered is given, and no source says who keys the record: those trained are officers of the regional, prefectoral and communal education offices, so entry may be away from the school. The schools aspect disagrees across dates: none in March 2021 (GIN-007), not published in March 2026 (GIN-014); the newer stands. The 2021 roadmap gives no period and falls outside the 36 months, so no current plan is held; finance is not stated. GIN-001 and GIN-002 are from the excluded source and set nothing.

short: Schools record each pupil in a national register, scaled up from 200 pilot schools in 2021; how many primary schools enter data is not known.
gaps: No count or share of primary schools entering data is published: the one figure, nearly 80% of learners in the registry (GMB-026, August 2025), is a share of learners. The sources disagree on pilot or live: the learner register is said to be scaled nationally since 2021, while GPE KIX in October 2025 (GMB-019) and DHIS2 in September 2024 (GMB-029) still call the SEMIS app a pilot; the register's value is written here, and the newest dated fact reads pilot. Level is named only in 2022. Finance is not stated within the 36 months, and no dated event falls in the last twelve. GMB-001 to GMB-004 are from the excluded source and set nothing.

short: The yearly school count ran on a new platform in 2025; whether schools keep a per-pupil record is not known, so no stage is set.
gaps: The only three evidence rows (GNB-001 to GNB-003) come from the excluded source and set nothing. No admissible row describes a record per learner that schools add to during the year, and no admissible dated statement says primary schools keep learner records on paper only.

short: Schools return a yearly count by questionnaire (2026); whether any keeps a per-pupil record is not known, so no stage is set.
gaps: The only two evidence rows (GNQ-001, GNQ-002) come from the excluded source and set nothing. No admissible row describes a record per learner that schools add to during the year, and no admissible dated statement says primary schools keep learner records on paper only.

short: Primary and secondary schools register each pupil on the national system (2026); how many primary schools do so, and any attendance entry, is not known.
gaps: No row describes schools entering attendance or results per learner during the year, in NEMIS or KEMIS. The schools figures disagree and none counts schools entering data: 65 per cent of primary schools had captured data in NEMIS and 90 per cent were submitting EMIS data (both 2021), while the newer rows (2024) give no share of schools, only about 60 per cent of primary learners registered; no figure is held for KEMIS primary schools. The last twelve months disagree too: KEMIS became the required platform and its validation engine went live (KEN-006, KEN-010), against outages in the Grade 10 selection and capitation paid on manually verified data (KEN-005, KEN-007). No admissible row gives a rural figure; KEN-011 is from the excluded source and sets nothing.

short: The Ministry said in 2026 that its school data system is paper-based and a per-pupil record planned; whether any pilot has begun is not known.
gaps: The paper statement is of the Ministry's existing system and names no level and no school count; LBR-005's booklet row does not use the word paper, and LBR-006 is from the excluded source and sets nothing. No row shows staff trained, equipment delivered, an agreement signed or pilot schools for a school-level EMIS or the learner ID system, which is planned and not in use; finance:domestic is the plan's 60 per cent framework, not a budget line shown.

short: A system launched in 2024 gathers school data by online survey; how schools keep each pupil's record is not known, so no stage is set.
gaps: evidence.csv holds no row for the country. systems.csv lists only census-class, single-function and unclassified systems, none shown to hold a record per learner that schools add to during the year.

short: A 2018 pilot tracked individual pupils in one hundred schools; their level, and whether it still runs, is not known.
gaps: The only admissible coverage fact is the 2018 pilot, which gives neither the schools' level (read as primary) nor who enters the records; nothing admissible is dated since, so whether the pilot still runs is not established. The governance rows are from 2018, outside the 36 months, and LSO-001 to LSO-003, including the statement that the pilot was scaled back and records are on paper, are from the excluded source and set nothing.

short: Every school has registered its pupils in a national per-pupil record since 2014; how many primary schools enter attendance or marks is not known.
gaps: No share or count of primary schools entering attendance or results: MAR-004's 10,000 establishments (2014) are all levels registering learners, and the newer MAR-011 gives no figure. Routine entry is shown only for lower secondary (MAR-005, MAR-006, newest levels fact S against P;S in MAR-002 and MAR-009); MAR-010 does not say who keys primary marks. Plan and finance not stated.

short: A pilot gave 180,000 pupils in one district a permanent number in 2026; whether any primary school beyond the pilot has enrolled is not known.
gaps: The 792 establishments (MDG-003) are the pilot district, all levels, with no total and primary not counted apart; it follows MDG-007 and MDG-009, which held none in December 2025. For the scale-up launched on 11 May 2026 only a target is held, no result, and the one school named is lower secondary. Who keys the record is not stated (MDG-002). No plan stated. MDG-006 is from the excluded source and sets nothing.

short: A donor project gave families cards for heads to scan pupils' attendance on tablets in 2020; whether any school does so is not known.
gaps: All admissible rows are one source of February 2020; nothing is held since, so governance (partner-owned and donor-financed in 2020, MLI-005 and MLI-006) and the last twelve months are outside their windows. No count or share of schools scanning attendance, and the one school named 'will digitize' in 2020 rather than is doing so. MLI-001, the statement of paper records, is from the excluded source and sets nothing.

short: A pilot tracking individual pupils was reported in 2025; which schools, how many and whether it has gone further is not known.

Governance is not held inside the 36 months: the ministry's ownership is dated May 2019 and the plan naming SEGI ran 2020-2025, ended before the as-at. MOZ-001 and MOZ-002 are from the excluded source and set nothing.

short: Pupil registration for 2026-2027 opened on a ministry platform in September 2026; who enters the records and in how many schools is not known.
gaps: The source does not say whether Siraj's pupil registration is a pilot or live, who keys the entries (the school or the parent), which level it covers or how many schools use it. No plan or finance is stated. MRT-001 is from the excluded source and sets nothing.

short: A per-pupil school record system was being designed in 2019; whether it was built or any school uses it is not known.
gaps: The only evidence is a needs-assessment and design mission of February 2019; nothing dated since says whether the system was built, piloted or used in any school, at which level, or how records are kept. Governance is not held inside the 36 months: the ministry's ownership is dated 2019.

short: Schools kept each pupil's record in paper registers made by hand in 2026; whether any digital record is being prepared is not known.
gaps: No row names a level, a school count or an owner, plan or budget for a digital learner record. MWI-001 to MWI-003 are from the excluded source and set nothing.

short: In 2018, 807 of 1,848 schools were connected to the national school system and 103 piloted daily attendance entry; anything since is not known.
gaps: Everything held dates from 2018: nothing inside the 36 months for governance or the 12 months for change. The 807 of 1,848 schools are connected to School-Link, not shown entering data, and cover all levels with no primary split; daily attendance entry is established only for a 103-school pilot. NAM-004 (routine) and NAM-007 (most schools on paper registers) disagree on how the record is kept. NAM-001 is from the excluded source and sets nothing.

short: School heads filled printed forms for the yearly school count in 2025; how schools keep pupils' records is not known, so no stage is set.
gaps: The only evidence row, NER-001, is from the excluded source and sets nothing. No admissible dated statement that primary schools keep learner records on paper, and no row on a system holding a record per learner.

short: A national learner number was launched in 2026 and issued first to examination candidates; whether any primary school enters learners' records is not known.
gaps: No row names a level in use, says who enters a learner's number or shows any primary school filling the register: the 1.9 million numbers of the first phase went to WAEC and NECO examination candidates, and extension to all learners is the next phase. short: Primary schools keep a profile per pupil with exam results, and a daily attendance app is live (2026); the share of schools is not known.

KARAME and the attendance tracking system name no school level, read as primary. short: The ministry counts schools by survey (2026); how primary schools keep their pupils' records is not known, so no stage is set.
gaps: Both evidence rows, SDN-001 and SDN-002, are from the source the study excludes and set nothing. No admissible dated statement that primary schools keep learner records on paper, and no admissible fact on any system holding a record per learner; systems.csv holds census-class surveys and EMIS pilots in state ministries that no source classifies.

short: A December 2025 brief describes paper-based school data collection; whether primary schools keep a per-pupil record is not known, so no stage is set.
gaps: SEN-001 and SEN-002 are from the source the study excludes and set nothing. The one admissible row, SEN-003 (2025-12, dated by publication), speaks of paper-based education data collection and isolated digital files at school and sub-national level generally: it does not name learner records, primary schools or paper only. short: In 2022-23 a rollout gave 300 primary schools tablets to enter each pupil's daily attendance; how many do so is not known.
gaps: The 300 is a count of primary schools in the Wi De Ya rollout phase, not of schools entering data, and no total of primary schools is given with it; nothing is dated after 2023 on its use, and the planned rollouts to 1,500 and 4,000 schools are not confirmed. short: A daily per-pupil attendance app was on trial in 42 schools in Puntland State in May 2022; what has happened since is not known.

short: Teachers reported each absent pupil by text message in 2024; the share of primary schools doing so is not known.

short: Schools sent data to the ministry's school-management system in 2023; whether primary schools keep a per-pupil record is not known, so no stage is set.

short: A per-pupil record has covered all 976 primary and secondary schools since March 2024; how many primary schools enter attendance or results is not known.

short: The ministry trained school leadership teams on its pupil record platform in 2026; whether any school enters attendance or results is not known.

short: Schools filled the yearly school count on paper in 2021; how primary schools keep pupils' records is not known, so no stage is set.

short: The ministry launched pupil numbering and designed its platform in 2023; whether any school yet uses it is not known.
gaps: No school is named as using the pupil-numbering platform and no pilot is reported: the 2023 launch and platform design (TGO-003) is followed by the April 2024 panel finding no clear evidence of student numbers, with collection still being developed (TGO-005). short: In December 2023, 92.7% of public primary schools were on the ministry's school system; how many enter attendance or results is not known.
gaps: No share or count of primary schools entering attendance or results: the 92.7% (4,322 of 4,662 public primary establishments, December 2023) is not said to be schools entering data, and the same deck puts the uploading of primary pupils' absences at 2%, of what it does not say. short: Heads and teachers in one council were trained on a school record system in January 2026; whether any primary school enters attendance is not known.
gaps: No source shows a primary school entering attendance or results after the directed start of the School Information System on 13 January 2026: the one dated account is of training in a single council, and the Mbeya account says what teachers are expected to do, not what is entered. The schools facts disagree (`none` for the planned tracking system in November 2025, `not-published` for the SIS in January 2026); no plan or finance is stated, and no count of schools is given.

short: In 2025, 58.9% of all primary schools uploaded pupils' enrolment details to the national register; whether any enter attendance or results is not known.
gaps: No source describes schools entering attendance or results: every row describes registration of learners, transfers and a yearly data upload. The owner facts disagree, the Auditor General's finding that the vendor runs administration and configuration (reported 9 June 2026) against the ministry as custodian and operator (8 June 2026, December 2025); no plan or finance is stated, and no rural share is held.

short: Schools record attendance and marks digitally and a national register holds each pupil, in 2025; the share of primary schools doing so is not known.
gaps: No share or count of primary schools entering attendance or results during the year is held: the 2025 rows publish none (ZAF-007, ZAF-013), and the 99.9% of July 2024 (ZAF-014) counts schools of all levels whose database was uploaded to LURITS, which disagrees with them only in kind. Nothing is held for the last twelve months, the Western Cape does not use SA-SAMS for source data, and ZAF-001 to ZAF-003 are from the excluded source and set nothing.

short: Schools report enrolment yearly on paper, by a 2025 account; how they keep pupil records is not known, so no stage is set.
gaps: The one evidence row (ZMB-001) is from the excluded source and sets nothing, so no admissible statement that learner records are on paper is held. The systems on file are a yearly census, single-function tools and one district's monthly and termly reports; none is a record per learner that a primary school adds to during the year.

short: The ministry said in 2026 its system tracks each pupil's absence and grades; how many primary schools enter them is not known.
gaps: The source does not say who enters the attendance and grades or where, and gives no count or share of schools in the Early Warning System; the stage rests on one news report of June 2026. It disagrees with the older facts (ZWE-007 of 2019, ZWE-008 of 2022), which state no learner-level system; the newest stands. No plan or finance is held, and ZWE-006 is from the excluded source and sets nothing.
